title: I’ve been paid—how much of the money can I actually spend?
snippet: When a client payment lands, your balance can look reassuringly healthy. Before you spend it, work out what is already committed to tax, costs and the quieter weeks ahead. The post I’ve been paid—how much of the money can I actually spend? appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

A client payment is not a spending limit. First account for VAT, tax, committed costs and the likely gap before your next payment. 

There is no tax percentage that works for every freelancer. Base your reserve on current year-to-date figures and your own circumstances. 

Your bank balance can overstate what is available when supplier bills, collaborators, subscriptions or other costs have not yet been paid. 

A deliberate personal transfer—regular or variable—is safer than letting each large invoice set your spending for the month. 

If the honest remainder is repeatedly too small, treat it as evidence to revisit rates, scope, payment terms or costs. 

The notification arrives: your client has paid. Your balance looks healthier and the immediate pressure eases. Then comes the harder question: how much of that payment can you actually spend? 

For a UK sole trader, the practical answer is: only what remains after allowing for VAT, setting aside a realistic tax reserve, identifying costs already committed and leaving enough cash to reach the next likely payment. That decision needs current records and a view of what is due next—not just the latest invoice or bank balance. 

This article focuses mainly on UK self-employed sole traders. A limited company is legally separate from its owner, and taking money out through salary, dividends or a director’s loan follows different rules. See GOV.UK guidance on taking money out of a limited company. 

The balance is not the spending limit 

For an employee, Income Tax and National Insurance are usually deducted before salary reaches their bank account. As a freelancer, you may receive the full value of an invoice and have to make the important decisions afterwards. 

A large payment may represent several weeks of work rather than one unusually successful day. The next commission may be smaller, delayed or unconfirmed. The apparent surplus may also need to cover illness, holidays or time spent finding new work. 

Australia-based freelancer Rosalyn Page separates money for tax, retirement, sick leave, annual leave and business costs before looking at the remainder. The rules differ in the UK, but the emotional effect will be familiar. 

“Using this system I often feel a bit disappointed when I see what’s left over,” she says. 

She calls it a reality check. A freelance rate may look high because it covers more than the hours spent producing the work, including obligations and benefits an employer might otherwise handle. The fee is doing several jobs before any personal spending begins. 

One payment can have several jobs 

A self-employed beauty studio owner featured in Money Diaries from Sage shows what this looks like in practice. In one week, £1,037.77 came into the business. It was not all hers to spend. 

In the beauty studio owner’s Money Diary, she counted £833.71 as spent or allocated. That included £395 reserved for future rent and tax and a £300 weekly payment to herself. After the week’s other business spending, £204.06 was added to the business balance. 

She had previously varied her personal income according to each week’s takings. Later, she introduced a regular transfer: “I now pay myself £300 per week regardless of how much or how little I earn that week.” 

Her amounts are not a formula for every freelancer. The reusable part is the decision: she gave the money different jobs before treating any of it as available for personal spending. A strong week no longer set her personal budget on its own. 

Money received is not personal spending money 

Three figures are easily confused: 

Money received is the cash that has arrived from a client. If you are VAT registered, it may include VAT you charged on the invoice. 

Profit is broadly what remains after allowable business expenses. For a sole trader, taxable profit—not the amount transferred personally—is central to the tax calculation. 

Available personal spending money is the cash you can take after allowing for tax, upcoming costs and the amount the business needs to retain. 

Suppose a photographer receives £3,000 for a commission. It may need to cover an assistant, travel and equipment hire, and could be the final payment for several weeks of work. It is £3,000 received—not automatically £3,000 of profit or personal income. 

For a sole trader, a personal transfer is not an allowable business expense and does not reduce taxable profit. Our practical guide to allowable expenses for self-employed people explains which business costs you may be able to deduct when calculating your taxable profit. 

Sense-checking a payment

What already has a claim on the payment 

Here’s what you need to consider.

Tax and VAT 

A single invoice cannot tell you how much tax to reserve. For a sole trader, Income Tax and National Insurance depend on taxable profit across the year, other income and personal circumstances. A percentage can be a working estimate, but it should come from current figures—not somebody else’s rule of thumb. 

The timing matters too. Payments on account can mean paying towards the next Self Assessment bill as well as settling a balancing payment. Check your HMRC account, software or accountant’s estimate before treating the reserve as spare cash. 

If you are VAT registered, the payment may include VAT you charged. Your VAT return determines what is payable after the relevant calculations, including eligible VAT you can reclaim. Until then, do not treat the VAT-inclusive balance as personal income. See GOV.UK guidance on charging and recording VAT. 

UK freelance writer and sole trader Dan Raywood uses a deliberately cautious rule of thumb. 

“When I started as a full-time freelancer, I was told to put aside a third of every earning. I’ve also heard about putting aside a quarter, but I err on the side of caution.” 

Dan’s approach provides a starting buffer rather than calculating his eventual liability. Your appropriate reserve may be higher or lower, so compare any percentage with current year-to-date figures and your expected tax bill. 

Business costs not yet paid 

Freelance costs do not always leave the account when the related income arrives. A collaborator may invoice later; software, insurance or a membership may renew next month; materials or travel may still need to be recorded. 

A London plumber in another Money Diary used merchant accounts to buy expensive materials before paying for them. His warning was that delayed supplier bills could make the business look richer than it was. The same problem arises whenever a committed cost has not yet reached the bank statement. 

An allowable expense may reduce taxable profit, but it still consumes cash. Both its tax treatment and payment date matter. 

Personal income and a buffer 

A large invoice can make a generous personal transfer feel affordable, but that transfer still needs to work when the following month is quieter. 

Dan uses separate accounts to make those boundaries visible. 

“I use a separate account to ‘hold’ the money I earn, and put an amount each time into another account for my tax return,” he says. 

The retained balance also helped during a quieter summer. Dan made sure each month held enough to cover his bills and living costs instead of allowing one stronger invoice to set his immediate spending. 

His arrangement is a personal cash-management system, not a universal formula. You might transfer a regular amount and review it against several months of results, or vary withdrawals while maintaining a minimum balance for known commitments. Separate accounts can make reserved money harder to spend accidentally, but they do not replace accurate records or an up-to-date tax estimate. 

What if there is not enough left? 

An honest calculation may leave less than you hoped. Do not improve it on paper by deleting the tax reserve, ignoring a supplier bill or assuming a client will pay early. 

Look upstream. Your rate may not cover the full cost of freelancing; the scope may have grown without the fee changing; payment terms may leave you carrying costs too long; or overheads may be squeezing personal income. Compare several months of real records before deciding which explanation fits. 

The beauty studio owner planned to review her £300 weekly payment after six months and adjust it if the business could not support it or had room for more. Choose a method, then test it against what happens rather than treating the first figure as permanent. 

Final thoughts

We always love a client payment, but the useful number is the remainder after tax, committed costs, personal income and the next gap between payments are visible. It may look disappointing, but it is also more honest. If it repeatedly falls short, you have evidence to revisit rates, scope, payment terms or costs before the tax bill or quiet month arrives. 

This article provides general information for UK freelancers and is not personal tax, accounting or financial advice. Rules and circumstances vary, so check current GOV.UK guidance or speak to a qualified adviser if you are unsure. 

Frequently asked questions 

			

			

	

Can I spend the full value of a freelance invoice? 

	

			

Usually not. First identify any VAT included, update your tax estimate, list costs already committed and decide what the business must retain until the next expected payment. The safe-to-spend amount is the remainder—not the headline value of the invoice or the current bank balance. 

	

	

How much should a freelancer put aside for tax? 

	

			

There is no percentage that fits every freelancer. For a UK sole trader, the amount depends on taxable profit across the year, other income and personal circumstances. Use current records, allow for payments on account where relevant, and check the estimate in your software, HMRC account or with an accountant. 

	

	

Does VAT count as income? 

	

			

If you are VAT registered, the VAT collected from a customer should not be treated as personal spending money. Your VAT return determines what is payable after the relevant calculations, including eligible VAT you can reclaim. Keep the gross payment and the amount actually available to the business conceptually separate. See GOV.UK VAT guidance. 

	

	

Should I pay myself a regular amount? 

	

			

A regular transfer can make personal budgeting steadier and stop a strong month from inflating your spending. A variable amount may suit an irregular business better. Whichever approach you use, base it on several months of income and costs, retain enough for known commitments and review the figure rather than assuming it will always remain affordable. 

	

	

What changes if I work through a limited company? 

	

			

A limited company is legally separate from its owner. Company money does not automatically become personal money when a client pays. Taking money out through salary, dividends, expense repayments or a director’s loan follows different rules, so use the company’s current figures and get advice when needed. See GOV.UK guidance on taking money out of a limited company.

title: How to stop freelance admin taking over your Sunday
snippet: Receipts, invoices, and payment checks can build up while you’re busy with client work. Use this weekly finance routine to keep the essentials moving and reduce the admin waiting for you at the weekend. The post How to stop freelance admin taking over your Sunday appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Book a recurring finance appointment during your working week.

Save receipts and send invoices as they happen, then use the weekly session to check for gaps.

Track money received separately from invoices still awaiting payment.

Record business costs and flag anything with uncertain tax treatment.

Clear any backlog one period at a time while keeping current records moving.

To stop freelance admin taking over your Sunday, give your financial paperwork a regular place in the working week. Record income and expenses, gather receipts, send invoices, check payments and review upcoming costs in the same order each time.

Some jobs are easier to finish as they happen. Save a receipt when it arrives, for example, or send an invoice when an agreed milestone is complete. 

Your weekly session then becomes a chance to check what’s missing and decide what needs attention. The aim is to make the work easier to repeat, including when client deadlines compete for your time.

Here’s what we talk about in this article:

Why does freelance admin end up on Sunday?

A client needs their revised designs by Friday. A receipt needs filing, but nobody is asking for it today. It’s easy to see which job gets your attention.

Repeat that choice across a week and Sunday becomes the first opportunity to work through everything you postponed. Before you can update your records, you’re searching emails, checking your bank account and trying to remember what a payment was for.

That reconstruction adds work of its own. A useful routine gives each document somewhere to go and each unfinished task a next action.

The problem isn’t limited to freelancers. Research from Sage found the average small business spends two days a month on financial admin, such as chasing invoices and late payments. That’s around 24 days a year.

The work outside customer-facing hours also appears in Money Diaries by Sage. In a 2022 diary, a Sunderland café owner described spending around three hours on banking, stocktaking and restocking on days that were supposed to be off. It’s a different business from freelancing, but a useful reminder to include the work behind the service when planning your week.

Here, freelance admin means the financial work behind your paid projects: recording payments and costs, saving evidence, invoicing, following up money owed and preparing information for tax. If you’re a UK sole trader, HMRC requires records of your business income and expenses for Self Assessment.

Making Tax Digital for Income Tax adds to this. It already applies to sole traders and landlords with qualifying income (gross income from self-employment and property, before expenses) over £50,000. It will apply to those over £30,000 from 6 April 2027, and over £20,000 from April 2028.

If it applies to you, you’ll keep digital records and send HMRC quarterly updates through compatible software, so a weekly routine also keeps you ready for each update.

What should you do in your weekly finance routine?

Erin Walls, founder and director of WallsMan Creative, an accountancy firm specialising in creative businesses, recommends making consistency the priority.

“We always tell our clients that the software or the system they use is secondary to consistency,” she says.

Her advice is to spend a little time on admin each Friday rather than leave it for a long Sunday-night session before a deadline: “You shouldn’t try to do a month’s admin in one go.”

Choose a time you can usually protect, such as Friday before client work or Wednesday after lunch. Allow enough time for your transactions: a short session may be enough when your records are current; catching up on a backlog will take longer.

At the SMB Advisory Board run by Sage, one business owner explained that they normally completed their accounts after a busy trading period. Having to prepare figures partway through that period disrupted their routine.

When choosing your weekly finance slot, account for your busiest delivery periods and decide when you’ll move it if client work intervenes.

Follow these seven steps.

1. Gather this week’s documents

Collect new receipts, supplier invoices and messages about client payments. Check the places you normally receive them, including email, online accounts and your wallet.

Store them in one consistent system. A photographer might keep studio-hire invoices and travel receipts in the same finance folder, organised by date.

Use names that help you recognise documents later. A date, supplier and short description can be more useful than a downloaded filename full of numbers.

HMRC’s examples of supporting records include receipts, bank statements and sales invoices.

2. Check which client payments have arrived

Compare payments received with your invoices. Record who paid, the amount, the date and which work the payment covers.

Keep partial payments visible. If an invoice is for £800 and £400 has arrived, record the payment without marking the whole invoice as settled.

Keep money received separate from money you’re still expecting. Your tax records must also follow the accounting method you use. Cash basis has been the default for sole traders since April 2024, and HMRC explains how it differs from traditional accounting.

3. Record costs and keep the evidence

Add business costs to your records while you can still explain what they were for. Keep the receipt or supplier invoice alongside the entry, or make sure you can find it easily.

For a cost connected to a particular project, note the project too. That can help you understand what delivering the work actually cost.

Recording a purchase doesn’t automatically mean you can deduct it for tax. Some purchases have both business and personal uses, and some need a closer check. HMRC’s allowable-expenses guidance explains that only the qualifying business costs can be claimed.

Flag anything uncertain for review instead of guessing.

4. Send invoices for work ready to bill

Check completed work against the payment arrangements you agreed. Have you reached a milestone, finished a project or completed a month covered by a retainer?

Issue the invoice at the agreed billing point. Include the information the client needs to process it, and record its payment due date. If it’s ready to send on Tuesday, there’s no need to wait for Friday’s admin session.

A London plumber featured in the Money Diaries from Sage described billing clients before leaving each job, helping him avoid catching up on invoicing at home after work.

5. Review unpaid invoices

Look at invoices approaching their due dates and those already overdue. Check your payment records before following up.

For an overdue invoice, refer to the invoice number, amount and agreed due date. Ask for an update on payment and keep a record of the response.

Separate ordinary reminders from invoices involving a dispute or missing information. Each needs a clear next action.

For more detail, see the Sage Advice guide to following up late payments.

6. Review your tax preparation

Check whether your income and expense records are current and whether the money you’re reserving for tax still reflects your circumstances.

If you use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, check when your next quarterly update is due.

Avoid treating every client payment as available spending money. Equally, don’t assume a single percentage will give every freelancer the right tax reserve.

If you’re unsure about your likely bill, use current official guidance or ask an accountant to help you estimate it. Keep tax money identifiable within your own system so you can distinguish it from money available for other costs.

7. Look ahead

Check expected payments, upcoming subscriptions, supplier bills and work reaching an invoicing milestone.

Regular bills are easy to lose track of. The café owner in the Money Diaries from Sage knew the payment for her coffee order came out every month, but it slipped her mind that it was due that week.

Write down the actions that follow: send an invoice, chase a missing document, ask about a payment date or check an unfamiliar cost.

A useful session ends with records you can understand and a short list of specific jobs.

What should your weekly checklist include?

Copy this list into your calendar appointment or task manager:

Gather new receipts and supplier invoices.

Match payments received to invoices.

Record costs and flag uncertain tax treatment.

Send invoices for work ready to bill.

Check unpaid and overdue invoices.

Review money reserved for tax.

Check upcoming payments and costs.

Write down any question needing advice.

How can you keep the routine going?

Make documents easier to collect between sessions. Save emailed invoices in the same place, capture receipts while they’re still legible and keep payment queries with the relevant invoice.

At the Small and Medium-sized Business (SMB) Advisory Board convened by Sage, one self-employed participant described returning to her accounting software each month and struggling to remember how she had handled a payment split previously.

It’s a familiar problem when finance is only one part of your job. Keep a short note of tasks you have to look up, so you can follow the steps next time instead of working them out again.

At Accountex Summit Manchester, DJH Head of Cloud Advisory Ryan Alderson described clients photographing train tickets as they travelled: “Their train ticket’s on there by the time they reach the next station.”

The same habit can help freelancers: capture a document while it’s in front of you, so your weekly finance session involves less searching and remembering.

Use the same task order each week so you spend less time deciding where to begin. If your tools can help with recurring invoices, reminders or transaction capture, check what they support and review the results.

If the same task keeps slipping, walk through it from start to finish. Can you save a receipt from your phone? Can you match a bank payment to the right invoice? Can you find a document without searching several inboxes? Fix the step that slows you down, then try it again during your next weekly session.

What if you’re already behind?

Choose one defined period to work through, such as the previous month. Gather its statements, invoices and receipts, then identify missing records and unpaid invoices.

Keep current records moving while you clear the backlog separately. Otherwise, the catch-up work can keep growing.

Prioritise urgent issues, including missed deadlines or payment problems. Ask for help where records are incomplete or your obligations are unclear. Don’t invent figures to make the paperwork look finished.

If you use an accountant or bookkeeper, agree who does what. Check who records transactions, matches payments, follows up missing information and prepares submissions, along with when they need your records. If you need more help than originally agreed, raise it early so you can discuss the work and any additional fee.

Final thoughts

It’s never too late to do things better with your business admin, and new habits are surprisingly easy to create. Getting on top of everything can also be one of the best feelings when running a business, and knowing that your admin is ticking over nicely creates the confidence for you to do more of what you love. 

Common questions about freelance admin 

			

			

	

Do I have to do financial admin every day? 

	

			

Not necessarily. Some tasks are easier to complete immediately, such as saving a receipt or sending an invoice. A weekly review helps you check that those smaller actions have left your records complete. 

	

	

Can I finish everything in 30 minutes? 

	

			

Possibly, once your records are up to date. It depends on how much activity you have. Allow more time initially and adjust the appointment to the work you actually need to do. 

	

	

How does Making Tax Digital affect a weekly routine? 

	

			

If Making Tax Digital for Income Tax applies to you, you’ll need digital records and quarterly updates to HMRC. A weekly review helps keep those records current and can reduce the catch-up work needed before each update. 

	

	

Can software help with the routine? 

	

			

Yes, with parts of it. Tools that capture receipts, import transactions or send recurring invoices can help. Check the information they produce: you still need to spot missing payments, duplicates and costs that need a closer look. 

	

	

Give the work a place in your week 

	

			

The receipt, unsent invoice and unanswered payment query each need a small action. Leaving them together until Sunday can make it harder to see where to start. 

Book your first finance appointment during the working week and use the checklist in this article to review the past seven days.
